eligibility_reason: The reflector is equipped with episodic memory that the model itself writes: p. 13 (Fig. 12/13) states 'there are diminishing returns to adding more episodic memories to the reflector when the model is allowed to augment its own memory with its own synthesis,' i.e. the agent generates and stores new memory content at run time. That store is then retrieved on later queries via BM25 similarity to condition subsequent audience-curation attempts (p. 4, Reflector subsection: 'we allow it to retrieve relevant solutions from a list of episodic memories ... using BM25 ... to find relevant solutions'). p. 3 additionally states generally that 'we explore the possibility of having LLMs update their memory based on the findings from the current user session.' This is a 2025 (record metadata), English, full-text-available paper, so I1-I4 all hold and no exclusion criterion applies: the system is a multi-agent LLM framework (not E6), memory is central to the title and the evaluated ablations rather than incidental (not E5), it is a primary contribution not a secondary study (not E4), and the store is agent-written, not a fixed corpus (not E3).

facets.justification: The primary, most heavily evaluated memory (Table 1, p. 4: 28-point accuracy gain on 88 queries) is described on p. 3 (Planner subsection) as 'a list of facts' serving as semantic memory, 'retrieved from a longer list based on their similarity to the user query with BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza 2009).' BM25 is lexical/term-based ranking, not embeddings, so vector_store does not fit; no schema, graph structure, file paths, or KV-cache reuse are described anywhere in pp. 1-4, 8, 12-14. Coded other: a BM25-indexed list with no further storage detail given. The secondary episodic-memory store used by the reflector (p. 4, p. 13) is the same kind of BM25-indexed list, also coded other in secondary_substrates.

For the primary (semantic-memory/facts) store, p. 3 states only, in general terms, 'we explore the possibility of having LLMs update their memory based on the findings from the current user session' and 'the benefits of self-learning to update this memory' — no transformation (append, edit, summarize, synthesize) is specified for this store in the given pages. The only concretely described write mechanism in the extraction — reflect-synthesize, where 'the model is allowed to augment its own memory with its own synthesis' (p. 13, Fig. 12/13) — applies to the secondary episodic-memory store used by the reflector, not to the primary store the main 88-query benchmark measures, so it is not used to code this axis.

p. 3 (Planner subsection): facts are 'retrieved from a longer list based on their similarity to the user query with BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza 2009).' This is a similarity-ranked retrieval rather than an exact filter, so it fits similarity_topk better than structured_query (defined as 'an exact query, not a ranking'); note the similarity metric is BM25 lexical scoring rather than dense embeddings, which the rubric's wording assumes, but no other listed value fits a ranked, non-exhaustive-context retrieval.

The headline result (p. 4, Table 1: '28 percentage points on a dataset of 88 filter-based queries') and the challenge-set result (p. 4 and p. 13, Fig. 12/13, a '10, more challenging queries' set) are both produced on benchmarks the authors constructed themselves, compared against ablated baselines (no memory, no verifier/reflector). No deployed system, external users, or real operating stakes are reported in the given pages beyond an internal 'higher user satisfaction' mention (abstract, p. 1) with no further detail. Coded validation, the conservative choice per the guide's tie-break rule.

p. 4 reports accuracy/precision/recall over the fixed 88-query benchmark across baseline vs. ablated configurations (Table 1, Table 2 referenced), and p. 13 (Fig. 12/13) reports the same over a fixed 10-query challenge set across iteration counts. Fixed task suites with reported scores, not a single manipulated condition with a control group in the controlled_experiment sense.

p. 2 contribution bullets: 'We introduce RAMP, a framework for audience curation, which incorporates verification and self-reflection modules to augment the base LLM performance.' RAMP is explicitly presented as an architecture organizing planner, actor, verifier, and reflector sub-agents (p. 1, Fig. 1), matching the guide's definition of framework as 'an architecture or a way of organising a system.'
